blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: DR RAVI JAYARAM (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
Dr Jayaram, could you introduce yourself, please, for the record?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm Dr Ravi Jayaram, I'm a consultant paediatrician at the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you. May I remind you, of course, that it is some time since you gave evidence last, but you are still bound, of course, by the oath or affirmation that you took on that occasion. And as you have just reminded the jury, you are still a consultant and you were a consultant in the paediatric department over the period with which this jury are concerned?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you. I want to ask you, please, about your involvement with a baby by the name of [Baby H].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Were you the on-call consultant for the children's unit on the night of 24 September 2015?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was the consultant on call that night, yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Did you attend, as a consequence of that, the afternoon handover that took place towards the end of that particular day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct. So at around 4 pm the consultant on call meets with the teams that have been looking after children through the day to get a handover of the patients that are around.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Forgive me if it's an obvious question, but the purpose of you being at that handover?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because I'm the consultant on call with ultimate responsibility for the care of children on the unit until the next morning I need to be aware of the patients that are in hospital, particularly those that are more unwell or may be at risk of becoming more unwell, just so that I have an overview of what might be about to happen over the next few hours.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Sorry, there's a difficulty -- yes, if you pull the microphone. That's it. That should be better.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Sorry about that. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Do you happen to recall what you were told about [Baby H] during the course of that handover?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I recall that [Baby H] had been born and had been on CPAP and had a pneumothorax, which essentially, I suppose, in lay terms is a collapsed lung. That means at some point she developed what's called an air leak, so as air was going into the lungs, a small hole would have been present in one of the alveoli, one of the air sacs, or a number of them, which meant that air then came out of the lung and accumulated in the space between the lung and the chest wall. And she'd been treated, I believe, with a chest drain, which means that that accumulation of air around the lung doesn't cause the lung to collapse down
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: further and compress the lung and stop gas going in out of the lung. But at the handover, she was considered to be stable.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. The purpose of the drain being to allow the air that's trapped to escape (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Absolutely. Because if that air remains in that space, each time a baby breathes more air will leak out of the lung, which means there's less space for the lung to inflate. And over time, if that accumulates, the lung then cannot inflate and it actually causes increased pressure inside the chest which can have an adverse effect on breathing and then on the circulation as well.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Did you in fact during the course then of that night when you were on call receive further communication concerning [Baby H]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I did. Again, referring back from my statement, it was -- in the early hours of the morning, the registrar called me because she was concerned about [Baby H] because, in spite of the chest drain being in, she was having difficulties with ventilation in terms of getting her oxygen saturations up.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We heard from that registrar yesterday. Do you recall the name of that registrar?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think it was Dr Alison Ventress.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you. Did Dr Ventress call you?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She called me. I can't remember the exact time, it's in my statement, but I think it was after 1 am.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Your recollection was 1.32.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Does that accord with your recollection?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, absolutely.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. Do you recall what you were told during the course of the call over and above what you just mentioned?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think -- I can't remember the timings of things without looking at my statement but I think that she'd told me that there were difficulties with getting [Baby H]'s saturations up in spite of turning up the oxygen with her being on CPAP. Alison Ventress had examined her and felt that she possibly had re-accumulation of air and I think at that point, but correct me
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: if I'm wrong, she'd done what was called a needle thoracocentesis. That's a procedure, when one suspects there's a pneumothorax, to drain air out rapidly in an emergency fashion. And I think at that point she'd done that when she called me first, but I will have to refer back to my statement.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Perhaps at this stage we don't need to do that but you mentioned the need for that to be done rapidly. We heard yesterday about tension pneumothorax -- different types of pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A tension pneumothorax means that each time a baby breathes in more air leaks out into the pleural cavity, which is the name of the space between the chest wall and the lung. So a simple pneumothorax means there's a small amount of air there but it's not getting bigger and sometimes simple pneumothoraces can be undiagnosed, sometimes they can be treated conservatively without any specific treatment. But in this situation, if a pneumothorax is considered to be compromising ventilation, then the air needs draining out rapidly.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: The definitive treatment is to put a chest drain in or a chest tube in. [Baby H] already had a chest tube in.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If you have a chest tube in and a pneumothorax is reaccumulating one has to assume either the chest tube is in a position that -- it's not, for whatever reason, draining air that's there or the chest tube could be blocked.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: But ultimately in an emergency situation, in a tension pneumothorax, it's a critical emergency because as that air in the wrong space accumulates it causes compression of the lung, it affects how blood can then return back to the heart, and how blood can be pumped around the body by the heart, and so it needs draining out as an emergency procedure.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Now, a chest tube itself, a chest drain or a pleural drain, can be put in reasonably quickly.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Can you pause there? Someone somewhere else is taking a note of what you say and I'm very grateful for the information, but --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You naturally speak very quickly.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm trying to learn to slow down!
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It's my fault, doctor, I'm here to assist.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: So you were saying that the drain -- I think you were saying that in certain circumstances the drain can stop working; is that --
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's unusual, but it can happen. So whether [Baby H] had popped another pneumothorax, so there'd been another air leak, whether the air was -- generally the cavity, the pleural cavity around the lung, is contiguous, so it's all one area. So in theory if there's air there, if you have a drain in that space, air should drain out.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Sometimes the tip of the drain could be against the chest wall or the lung and a drain can get blocked, but if you have a chest drain in and air appears to re-accumulate, you need to get that air out and then think later about why that air wasn't coming out of that drain. But the important thing is to get that air out.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Is there a way that you can tell whether the drain is working?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You can look at the drain so the drain itself --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Slow down a bit.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The drain itself -- there's two ways you can tell. So the original way these things used to work is that drains were connected to what was called an underwater seal, so you could actually see bubbles of air coming out of the end of the drain into water and you could see, as the baby breathed, a column of air going up and down that told you that the drain was patent, that it was open, and the child was breathing.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: There are also mechanisms which we used here called flutter valves, so there's a valve that goes on the end of the chest drain with a little rubber or plastic valve and you can see that flutter as the baby breathes -- and if the flutter valve is moving you know that the drain must be patent, it must be moving. So that's how you know a drain is working.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: In terms of diagnosing a pneumothorax, in a small baby we have a technique using a thing called a cold light. So it's a light source that doesn't generate heat and when you put the cold light on to the chest wall, ordinarily, because the lung is inflated and there's tissue there, it doesn't light up. In a pneumothorax, because the chest cavity is full of free air that's not in the lung, it tends to light up. The phrase people use is it lights up like a Hallowe'en pumpkin, just to give you an idea of what it looks like, and you compare the two sides. And certainly if you see the chest light up like that when you
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: do a cold light you have to make the assumption that there is a pneumothorax that needs -- that is significant.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We have actually seen a video of cold light, so thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's very helpful, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That just provides an oral description of what we've seen.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Just going back to the drain and when you were talking about fluttering, if the drain were to stop fluttering what would that tell you?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: If a drain stops fluttering it suggests that as the baby is breathing air isn't coming out through the drain.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Now that can actually happen if the pneumothorax has resolved, so if the lung has re-inflated completely and there's no more air leak, and actually the drain -- if there isn't really any significant amount of air coming into the pleural space you will see the drain stop fluttering. And in the clinical context of that if a baby is well and is getting better from a respiratory point of view, one could infer that actually the lung has reinflated.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Slowing down again a little, sorry.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But in the context of a baby where the oxygen requirement is increasing and we're having increasing difficulty, having to turn up the oxygen and the saturations are dropping, it can also be a sign that the drain, for whatever reason, is no longer draining air.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Right. So --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And that could be a blockage, it could be the drain is misplaced.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So the information from Dr Ventress was that [Baby H] was deteriorating?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Did she mention the chest drain at all (overspeaking) —
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember at what point she told me but I was aware that it had been noted that the valve was not fluttering.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And were you aware or not at that stage that she had either performed a thoracocentesis or --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think when she called me she'd performed -- I think — and again it's the timings, but I think at that point she had performed thoracocentesis and had drained a significant amount of air out.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So air coming out and the drain not fluttering?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, which suggests there was re-accumulation of a pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you. Did you attend?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I did. I can't remember exactly what time, I think it was before 2 am.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Well, we'll go to your note, if we may, because I hope that's the most reliable source in these circumstances.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Can I ask Mr Murphy, please, to go to tile 76.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we scroll down, we can see, towards the end there of Dr Ventress' note, what was happening before your arrival. If we could concentrate, please, on what you did, and if we go down to your note, it's written in retrospect at 4.55. But you've indicated there that you were called at 1.32 and you arrived at 1.50. Could you take us through your note, please --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'd made the comment that the story from Alison Ventress, the registrar, was that [Baby H] had been gradually deteriorating and then suddenly deteriorated, with her oxygen saturations going low and she looked pale with poor chest movement. The cold light had been put on and it looks like the left chest looked bright, suggesting there was free air. Dr Ventress had done a needle thoracocentesis and had aspirated quite a lot of air but the chest was still moving poorly.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We then organised a chest X-ray, which showed a left tension pneumothorax. That means that there was an accumulation of air and the position of the heart and the structures in the middle of the chest had been pushed to the other side.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: At that time the existing chest drain was looked at.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: It didn't look like there were any -- it didn't look like there were any obvious blockages in it. Because that pneumothorax was still present and it appeared to be under tension, we did a
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: further needle thoracocentesis in a different area, so the fourth interspace -- what that means is between, basically, the third and fourth ribs -- and aspirated more air.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. So that's another needle into the baby to release air in a slightly different position?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: That was based on the X-rays that you had seen?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Based on the X-rays and the clinical picture. So if she had been improving we would have perhaps not done that, but we'd seen, in spite of the needle thoracocentesis and the chest drain being in, she still had evidence of a tension pneumothorax. So that was an emergency procedure to try and aspirate some of that air, to give the lung a chance to inflate.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If we could just pause there and have a look at the Xrays that you would have seen during the course of that period. If we can look first at tile 48, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Bearing in mind you arrived at 1.50, this is an X-ray that was taken at 1.40. Is this the X-ray that you were describing to us?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that would have been the one I was just describing.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So one can see there is a chest drain, which is the tube that's coming out of the left side of the chest with the curl(?) on. One can see the needle that's in the top and the pneumothorax -you can see a rim if -- just where the cursor is now you can see a rim going down where the lung looks blacker and there's no lung markings, so that's a pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: But if one looks at the size of the left hemithorax, the left side of the chest compared to the right, you can see, I think quite clearly, even if you're not an X-ray expert, that it just looks bigger and that's basically because there's a large amount of air in there and a lot of that air is probably anterior, so although the rim of the pneumothorax looks relatively thin, you can see also that the heart has been pushed slightly across the right-hand side as well.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. Just pausing there, so as we look at the page, it's on the right-hand side of the picture?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: On the right as we look at it.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And by the view of the air being anterior, that's towards the front of the chest, is it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, anterior means the front of the chest. Obviously this X-ray is looking front to back, so you can see certainly a rim of pneumothorax there. If one looks down to the bottom there are lung markings all the way out to the edge, but you can see also that that half of the thorax is much bigger than the other half and that's basically because of accumulation, it's pushing the diaphragm, which is the muscle that separates everything in the chest from everything in the abdomen, it's pushing the diaphragm down.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If we pause there. We can see, I hope I can put it this way, sort of a cream-coloured border and it rises from right to left as we look at the picture; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: When you say cream-coloured?
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I think you're pointing at it. Thank you, Mr Murphy, for rescuing me. Is this where the diaphragm would be?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that's the diaphragm. Where the cursor is now is following -- is at the lateral end of the diagram. So where that sort of whiteness is. So the line between white and black is where the diaphragm is.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And we can see it's much higher on the other side.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You can see also it just looks blacker from the other side as well, which is a sign that there's more air there outside of the lung.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I wonder if we could go back to your note, please, which is at 76, by way of reminder.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think we'd reached the foot of page 1. If we can just check there's nothing else you need to -- I think you mentioned the fourth space at the bottom on the left side. It says something aspirated?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Air was aspirated."
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you. If we go on to page 2, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So in spite of this, in spite of draining this air, she continued to have poor chest movement and poor air entry. She was on a ventilator and then she suddenly dropped her saturations. So we'd treated the pneumothorax in the sense that we had a chest drain in, we had two needle thoracenteses and she dropped her saturations. And in that situation we then have to think, well, why are the saturations dropping.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So we removed the endotracheal tube, which appeared to be blocked with a mucus plug. And after the endotracheal tube was taken out she was bagged up. That means we used a self-inflating bag with a rubber mask/silicon mask over her nose and mouth and actually ventilated her quite easily and she was re-intubated by Dr Varghese, who's one of the SHOs.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you. Pause there again. Second drain.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, she hadn't had a second drain at that point.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So the air had been released --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: With the needle thoracocentesis.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: It didn't seem to fix the problem so the ventilation was checked and there was (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It looked like there was a (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- ET tube. But that was resolved by use of the mask that you told us about?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We removed that tube, then hand-ventilated her with a bag and mask, and then re-intubated her. And then when she was re-intubated she was put on to the ventilator settings that we can see here, so pressures of 24/5. That means that the ventilator was delivering a constant background pressure of 5 centimetres of water, which is kind of standard for a baby with respiratory distress syndrome. We have to deliver that background pressure because if it's not there actually there's a tendency for the airways internally to collapse down.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And each breath she had was delivered at a pressure of 24 centimetres of water, which is enough to move the chest and inflate the lungs at a rate of 40. Where it says "T in 0.45"(?) that means each breath we gave her lasted for 0.45 of a second. And she was in roughly 40-50% oxygen. And then we repeated her chest X-ray, both to check the position of the tube but also to see what was happening with the lung.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you to pause there. We'll see if we can look at that X-ray, please, which I think is at tile 55. This is timed at 2.29, doctor.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So when you look at this, you can see that the rim of pneumothorax at the top is still present but not as great but the lung -- the lung field is still bigger.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So certainly from a ventilation point of view she was more stable than she was. But we put a second chest drain in. Number
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: 1, after this, because you don't want to be leaving needles in. And given that the pneumothorax had re-accumulated we wanted to be sure we didn't want it to re-accumulate again.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So the pneumothorax hadn't resolved completely but it was better than it was but there was a single chest drain in and we felt that actually putting a second one in would be appropriate at this time.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: You discussed that between you?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. It was my decision to do that but we agreed.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If we go back to your notes then please at 76. We've moved into page 2 now.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So in terms of putting in a chest drain there are different techniques and equipment available. The more traditional/old-fashioned way is to use a more sort of surgical method where we dissect down, using a scalpel, cut through the skin, down to -- through the muscle, down to the pleura, and then we insert a drain with artery forceps, which are -- I'm thinking how to describe them -- very thin forceps. We hold the end of the drain and push it in through the pleura, which is the lining of the chest wall, between the chest wall and lung, and get that drain into the space.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We prefer these days to use what's called a pigtail drain, which is put in using a technique called the Seldinger technique. That involves putting a needle on a syringe and slowly inserting that needle between the ribs, aspirating/pulling out on the syringe as we go, until we hit air and aspirate air. At that point we take the syringe off the needle, leave the needle in.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We put a thin wire through the needle and take the needle out. So we now have a direct passage with a wire into the pleural cavity, the space between the chest wall and the lung.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We use a tool called a dilator, which is a plastic tube to make that track a big bigger. We take that out and then we insert the drain over the wire, and then we take the wire out and then the drain is secured and connected to a seal.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And I think it's easier to put those in. In my training we didn't really have those available so I've done several oldfashioned drains and, for whatever reason, no pigtail drains were readily available, so we put in an 8 gauge Argyle catheter, which is an old-fashioned chest drain, and I described there how we put that in.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Can I ask you to pause there and actually read what the note says.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So we used an 8 gauge -- 8 fringe(?) Argyle catheter and we made an incision in the fifth interspace, in the anterior axillary line. That's an anatomical description for -- the anterior axillary line is if you --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Nice and slowly, please, doctor.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, sorry.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If you drew a lien from the front of the armpit downwards, that's to sort of say where, on a vertical plane, we inserted the line and it's in the fourth -- what did I say? The fifth interspace. "Blunt dissection" means we make a small incision and rather than cutting all the way down with a sharp scalpel, once we're through the skin, we use the forceps to gently tease the tissues apart and then we basically advance and make a hole in the pleura, the membrane that separates the chest wall from the chest cavity, and then use those forceps to insert the drain in.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Once it is in, it is then connected to an underwater seal, and we saw that this was oscillating -- going up and down -- with breathing, which means we know it's in the right position. And then it was sutured in with a size 3 silk suture.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Before we move on from there then, you have described to us in detail how it's put in. I think you mentioned -- does it you say "No Cook drain available"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Just scroll back up again. The pigtail drains are manufactured by a company called Cook and there's different manufacturers, so they are the ones that we would normally have in stock at that time.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: There just happened to be none available?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: None available.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So an alternative was used?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And we needed to get one in reasonably quickly.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Just towards the end of your description you mentioned how it went into the water and you could see movement.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Could you just explain that to us?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So imagine this is a small bottle of water (indicating) and the end of the drain goes into that water (inaudible). What we will see is -- with respiratory movements we will see a column of water moving up and down the end of the tube that's in there. And that indicates that the drain is in the right place and it indicates that the drain is patent, it indicates that actually the drain -- the -- it indicates that the drain isn't blocked.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. Is there a term for that movement up and down?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Oscillation or swinging is the more sort of colloquial term for it.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Thank you. Then we can see that --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. We've heard in fact this morning, but you will be aware of this, please confirm, that in the early hours of 25 September, just following the chronology, Dr Jayaram, who was on duty overnight, was called out and fitted a second chest drain to [Baby H].

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Well, during the 25th I did.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember all the times exactly.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: All right. Can I ask you, first, please, about a -- do you recall a conversation with Dr Harkness on the 25th about [Baby H]'s condition?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- but at some stage I would have known what he was going to do.

blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: knowing that [Baby H] was experiencing problems with her breathing, needing, slightly unusually, two chest drains, I felt that it was appropriate to try and maintain a good level of haemoglobin, so agreed to go ahead with a blood transfusion.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. If we go next, please, to tile 160. We will see the notes of the afternoon's events that involved you, Dr Gibbs. blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Would that be consistent with your recollection? That's 3 o'clock in the notes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Well, it's at some time in the afternoon, but Dr Harkness has recorded it at 3 o'clock, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. If we scroll down, please, and I think you were aware of this, but there was an incident recorded at 16.45 when [Baby H] suffered a desaturation.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And I think that's your handwriting at the bottom of the page.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Just before my handwriting there's an entry by Dr Austin, one of our registrars, and in it she says, the third line down of her entry:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "ETT removed by N/S [nursing staff] [something] blocked [or query blocked]."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the nurses had removed the endotracheal tube, which is the tube down into the windpipe through which [Baby H] was being ventilated, because they thought it had blocked. blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And then Dr Austin has written "ETT replaced". So she's put another one in and asked for a chest X-ray and I have now recorded what I have seen on the chest X-ray as well.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I wonder if we could pause there, please, and go to tile 158. We saw from your note that you arrived at 5.45. This is an X-ray taken at 5.25, about 20 minutes before. I don't know

blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Thank you. If we can go back to your notes, please. If you could explain to us, please -- I'm hoping it's the second page --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think that's the end of my entry there. I've signed it at the bottom.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Your signature is cut off. Could you explain your entry to us, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right. So it says:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "ETT withdrawn..."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the tube that she was being ventilated through was withdrawn:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "... 0.5 centimetres prior to the chest X-ray because of decreased [that's the arrow down] air entry on the left."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So because we couldn't hear or I couldn't hear air entry very well on the left, there's various reasons why that might be so. But a common reason is that the tube is a little too low. If an endotracheal tube is pushed too far down a windpipe it tends to go down into the right lung -- anatomically the right lung's tube is more in line with the windpipe -- and that's why it was pulled back a little.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then it says:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "... to 8 centimetres at the lips."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then the X-ray had shown a satisfactory position of this ET tube, so it had been right to pull it back a little. It says:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Darker appearance in the left hemithorax."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the left side of the chest was a little darker but you couldn't see a lung edge. That suggests there's still a pneumothorax but only a thin layer of air around the outside of the lung. If there's a lot of air around the lung, the lung collapses down and you can see the edge of the lung. The only way you could tell there was likely to be a small pneumothorax at this stage on the X-ray was because it looked a bit blacker on the left side compared to the right.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Then it says "cold light". I think it says -- the code number, but "cold light normal". I'm fairly sure that says. I put "normal" in capitals.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We've heard a little about cold light tests and seen a video. So you were satisfied that what you saw was normal. Could you read the next line?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, what I saw on that X-ray -- there is a pneumothorax but it's not causing a tension problem, and the lung looks fully expanded. Also, although there was a small pneumothorax there on the chest X-ray, the cold light did not detect it because it can't detect all pneumothoraces, particularly small ones.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So a diagnosis for a pneumothorax comes from the X-ray rather than the cold light?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The X-ray is more sensitive than a cold light.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Cold light is indicative perhaps?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes and a cold light you can perform immediately on the neonatal unit, whereas an X-ray takes time to be taken, and then to be processed so you can see the picture. So a cold light is a quick assessment, a chest X-ray is more accurate but slightly slower assessment.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Your next line begins with a "left" again.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is it "left"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, "Left standard", and that means non-pigtail drain.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Earlier someone had called that the trocar drain as opposed to the pigtail drain, which is also called a Cook drain. So one of the chest tubes, the left standard non-pigtail drain, which is the one Dr Jayaram had put in during the previous night, had moved outwards. When I say it moved outwards, an X-ray earlier from that day, about 4.30 in the morning, had shown that the tube was well inserted into the chest.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: This X-ray, about 12 hours later -- well, 5ish in the afternoon, had shown the tube looks further out of the chest. It's still in the chest but it's moved a bit so I have then written down:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Fixed more securely to chest wall to try and prevent it moving any more."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So to stop it falling out.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: You detected some movement, movement out of the body?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, compared to the previous chest X-ray roughly 12 hours earlier.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Did anyone in particular draw your attention to that or did you notice that yourself?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I noticed it myself.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Other people might have noticed it. Dr Austin, the registrar, might have noticed it, but I noticed it myself and I recorded it in my observations here.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. I'm just going to pause there if I may.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Are there any potential consequences of a chest drain moving out in that way?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The main worry is it moving out completely and falling out and therefore being useless. So that's why I fixed it so it wouldn't move anymore. The answer to, are there any other consequences, is: it depends. A chest drain has a hole at the end and along the side of it near the top of it, the tip of it, so it drains from several places. If it's moved across the chest, it should still be effective at draining any air that shouldn't be there on the outside of the lung. But the worry is if it keeps on moving out, it'll become ineffective and fall out completely.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So it hadn't become ineffective, it was still functioning at this stage, it was still well inside the chest but had moved several centimetres from a previous X-ray.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Any risk to the internal structures by a chest drain moving in that way?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not that I am aware of. You wouldn't want to keep on pushing and pulling on a chest drain, and you wouldn't do that, so you're pushing it in and pulling it out the chest because that would be rubbing against the lung.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And also, if you pushed it very far into the chest, you're pushing against the heart. But at this stage the chest drain was moving outwards away from the heart and across the lung. But I
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: wouldn't have expected that to cause any problems as in trauma, damage, to [Baby H] at all. It's just the worry that it may go out further and become ineffective and fall out.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So it wouldn't be preventing a pneumothorax or draining a pneumothorax if it has fallen out.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So that, as you've pointed out, is the end of your note for that particular visit to [Baby H] that evening.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But I think you were consultant on call that night as well?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is it right that -- and we heard from Dr Ventress yesterday -- in the early hours of 26 September she called you as you were on call?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Do you recall what you were told by Dr Ventress at that stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Dr Ventress was experiencing -- [Baby H] was experiencing difficulties with her ventilation. I think from an hour or two before midnight, so the end of the 25th, Dr Ventress had been concerned about [Baby H] dropping her oxygen levels intermittently and she had manoeuvred one of the drains to try and improve any drainage of a pneumothorax. blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm not going to ask you to guess. If we can go to tile 216, please. We have there the note. Really, I'm interested in what you understood to be the position when you -- you did then go into the unit, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: expect if you have a tension pneumothorax, so the tension pneumothorax needed to be treated.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Dr Ventress had tried to treat it by manipulating the drain and I'm not sure, because it was done so many times, whether she had inserted -- no, she hadn't at this stage inserted a needle into the chest again, but she had tried to drain it through the drain.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. Did you look at that X-ray when you arrived on the unit?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I wonder if we could go, please, to tile 200. This was taken just before 11 o'clock.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So maybe a couple of hours before, I think, the telephone conversation with me at about 1 in the morning of the 26th, yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And the two chest drains can be seen on the left side.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Does my pointer work here?
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes, thank you for reminding me. We've connected a mouse that should enable you to point things out.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You can see a pigtail -- and you can see why it's called a pigtail, a curly tail, chest drain. Here is the straight -this is the one Dr Jayaram had inserted, this is the one the day before Dr Harkness had inserted.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That's the tube through which -- the endotracheal tube through which [Baby H]'s being ventilated. This other line running down here is just a nasogastric tube going into the stomach.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The main problem on this X-ray is that the heart, which -- this is mainly the heart down here. That's part of the thymus there. The heart should sit slightly to the right and mainly to the left in the chest and it's shunted across to the right-hand side of the left, it should be more than in the middle and left side.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: This is a normal sort of appearance of a lung on the right, just a very faint greyish appearance. Here you can see there's a lot more blackness around here. That blackness is air, it's not air inside the lung, which would look like this on the right, it's
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: air outside the lung, which is why it looks a lot blacker, and the lung is compressed, collapsed down underneath that, which is unusual because there are two chest drains in the chest that should be draining air out of this side of the chest, air that's outside the lung, and yet these are not effective enough.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. So if we can perhaps -- that's what you saw when you arrived. Can we go to your note next, please, which is at tile 228. If you could explain your note to us, please. I think you already embarked upon that process because it reads:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Chest X-ray shows re-accumulation of --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Left tension pneumothorax. Most air collecting medially, and that means to the middle of the chest, to the inner side of the left lung, and I've even described that further in brackets.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That means against the mediastinum, the mediastinum being the central structures in the middle of the chest.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Two existing chest drains, and I say:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Blocked with yellow serous fluid and unable to obtain air."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: In other words, we've talked before about the tube showing fluttering, which means air is coming out of them. There's no fluttering or bubbles coming out of them, despite aspirating, sucking on the drains. At this stage [Baby H] was needing a lot of oxygen, 80 to 100% O2, to maintain sats in the mid-90s. So at least that was providing good, satisfactory, safe oxygen saturations levels in her blood, but needing a lot of oxygen to do that.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The pressure now has increased to 27/4. I think a figure we saw a bit earlier from earlier in the day was 20/5. Now it's gone up from 20 to 27, which you expect because the tension pneumothorax causes extra pressure inside the chest, pressing on the lung from the outside, making it more difficult to ventilate. If [Baby H] was breathing by herself she'd find it very difficult to breathe against that pressure, so we needed a much higher pressure on the ventilator to achieve adequate ventilation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I think the next line beginning "plan" indicates what you concluded?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Plan. Needs further chest drain"
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And then:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Anteromedially sited."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So that means -- antero, to the front, and medially, to the middle of the chest. The difficulty, though, is that the air seemed on the X-ray to be collecting in the middle of the chest and towards the front of the chest. We try to avoid as far as possible inserting a chest drain right through the front of the chest, partly because you may hit major structures like the heart and great vessels in the chest going into the middle, but also from a cosmetic point of view, which is a long-term consideration, although the immediate consideration is to help a patient and as a life saving measure you might do things that have consequences long-term.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But long-term, any scarring from the chest drain looks more obvious in the front of the chest and may interfere with breast development in a girl, so we try to insert the chest drains at the outer side of the chest. But this was a challenge to get the chest drain from the outer side of the chest, but to get the end of it in the right place inside the chest.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right, okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And I just describe how I inserted a chest drain there.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is it unusual to insert a third chest drain in these circumstances?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I have only ever done it once in my career and that was this night.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And why?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: And I'd never heard of other patients needing -- there may be other patients that need three chest drains.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I've never heard of another patient needing three chest drains on the same side. I have been involved with patients needing a chest drain, one on each side, but never needing three together on the same side.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So there are two already in place.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: We've heard between the fifth -- the fifth and seventh spaces to the left side.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Why did you need, did you feel, to take this unusual course?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because despite these two chest drains being present in [Baby H], she was still developing -- had developed yet another tension pneumothorax, which is a potentially life-threatening complication. We could see on the chest X-ray there was air collecting but probably, and we have to assume this, not in an area where the two existing chest drains were able to drain it. So I inserted the chest drain, as I say here. I put fourth, crossed out fifth, around the fourth or fifth, and it's quite difficult in a little baby, even in an adult, but difficult in a small baby to count exactly which rib space you're in. So it was around the fourth or fifth space. But what I did, slightly differently, was more anteriorally, more to the front of the chest, where the air seemed to be, but still keeping on the outer side of the chest.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Just so we understand, you're indicating -- obviously the recording won't pick it up. You indicated that I think the two were in the area under the arm; would that be right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, on the lateral side, outer side of chest.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And yours in relation to those was closer to the centre?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was in a similar position to the two existing drains but slightly more anteriorally, more towards the centre.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But, for reasons I've said, you try -- I would try, and one is advised to try, to avoid putting a chest drain right through the centre of the chest. So it was still at the side of the chest, but more towards the end, more anteriorally, and when I inserted it I try to -- and there's a wire you use to insert the chest drain with, to angle that wire to the front of the chest.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Again, because, as you've told us, there are vital structures in there that require care?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So you mentioned a Seldinger technique?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Seldinger is the person who invented it. It's the name of the wire used to insert the chest drain.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. At the end of your note, you were aiming to site proximal end?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Could you read the last couple of words?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The proximal end, the inner side, to site it anteriorally and medially to the front and the middle of the chest.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: All right. "Underwater seal" is the next line. Could you explain that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The outer end of the drain that's hanging out of the chest is placed under water so you can see air bubbling out, but also that's a seal, it prevents air being sucked into the chest and making a pneumothorax re-accumulate. So it's a one-way valve mechanism to let air out of the chest but not into the chest, and also by the bubbles you can see and confirm air is being drained out of the chest.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: The drain there is described as swinging. Is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: What does that mean?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It means the water level was moving up and down as -- I was going to say [Baby H]'s breathing in and out but actually it's the ventilator doing it for [Baby H]. As the ventilator breathes in and out for [Baby H], the water level swings up and down, showing that the tube is patent, not blocked, so doing its job.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. The next line, please. Is that volume?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Volume/pressure. That's press. But volume pressure loops show improved compliance. On the ventilators we were using you can show little graphs, electronic graphs, which you can use to interpret how well you're ventilating a patient and how stiff a patient's lungs are, and this shows better compliance, so the lungs were moving better with the ventilator after putting this third chest drain in. That says FiO2, the amount of oxygen has dropped. It was 80 to 100%. It's now down to 30%. So there'd been a marked improvement in [Baby H] having inserted this three chest drain.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. That's in relation to the amount of oxygen in the air with which she is being ventilated?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So that's reduction in the need for oxygen?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, come down from 80 to 100% down to 30%.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Is that last note, is that for chest X-ray?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, to look at the position of the chest drain.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Did you look at the chest X-ray that followed?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Um... I did, but I haven't written any comment down here.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: All right. Can we go, please, to tile 229? This may or may not be the one. This is timed, I think, at 2.30 am.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Tell us what you can see on that, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'll try and use the pointer.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Please do once the screen settles down.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So previously, we saw in [Baby H]'s chest X-ray one long straight drain and one pigtail, curly, drain. This is now the third drain. It's a curly one but the way it's been cut, you can't see the coils as well as this top drain. But it's the one I've tried to insert more anteriorally and more medially. Having a pigtail, the curly bit, slightly prevents you getting it to exactly where you want because it coils up on itself inside the chest. But anyway this is more anteriorally nearer to the front of the chest.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Now we can see the chest -- the heart here with the thymus at the top. We don't have to, but if we've got the two X-rays side by side. It's moved to the left-hand side, it's not as thrust over to the right-hand side as it was before, and here we can see a left lung that's now fully expanded, not that different to the right lung. And there's no blackness like out here, there's no blackness around it. Before, the blackness was up against the edge of the heart and in the middle here. That has disappeared. It's been drained away. That was air that was outside the lung, compressing the lung, has now gone.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So as of -- if we can just remind ourselves of the time on that X-ray, 2.30. As of 2.30 what does that X-ray tell you about [Baby H]'s condition as far as it can in itself?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just from the X-ray, there's no pneumothorax and both lungs look well expanded, but again we don't -- we need to look at [Baby H] herself, her other observations and so on. But it shows there's no pneumothorax here. So the third chest drain has been very helpful and we knew that from the way the oxygen had come down and all the parameters indicating how easy or difficult it is to ventilate a patient had improved in [Baby H].
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. If we come out of that tile, please. I want to ask you about tile 231 for the sake of completeness.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It would appear that you have prescribed a medication called lidocaine. Is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Could you explain that to us, please? Lidocaine hydrochloride.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Could I see the time here? Administered...
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: It looks like it's administered at 2.36 and filed at 2.36. So shortly after that X-ray was taken.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Mm... Oh, the lidocaine is a local anaesthetic and it is given by injection before undertaking a painful procedure. So I would have assumed I had given lidocaine, injected it, before inserting the chest drain. What I'm pausing about now, and I haven't looked at this for a long time, in fact I don't recall seeing this particular prescription since 7 years ago when it happened. The timing is slightly odd. You give the local anaesthetic before you insert the chest drain.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I'm not quite sure why the chest drain has been inserted and now there's a local anaesthetic here. What does sometimes happen is that we give a medication and then we record it later on the computer, and this is a computer recording, so sometimes the time of a medication is not exactly the time it was given. It looks like it is, but it's the time it was recorded as having been given.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Well, we can see that the third drain is in at 2.30.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Your recollection is that you administered that particular medication before inserting the third chest drain?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So we know it must have been before 2.30 and it's entered on to the computer a little after you've checked the Xray.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, because in order to insert a chest drain -- I know in a way it sounds bad that we say -- and it does happen in medicine. We say this medicine was given at 2.32 and I'm telling you now that I think it was given before 2.32. But to insert a
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: chest drain, you put a gown on, you put gloves on, you do it as a sterile procedure, and you cannot then go to the computer and start typing up the medication you're giving at the same time, so that's why sometimes entries are made after the event.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Very good. Okay. So by the sound of it then, the X-ray has been taken, the third chest drain has done the job, you've updated the computer with the medication. Did you stay on the unit at that stage, did you continue to monitor [Baby H] or did you leave?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I left because I think I was called back shortly after.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. Do you remember where you were when you were called back?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, unless I've written it down.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: No, all right. Do you remember why you were called back?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, because [Baby H] had deteriorated again.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. Again, just as far as your understanding was, the message you received, what did you understand to be the problem?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A very serious problem, that [Baby H] was requiring cardiopulmonary resuscitation, including adrenaline. So she had collapsed in that sense.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. The significance of adrenaline?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's used in cardiac arrest. In babies, though, sometimes the heart has not stopped completely. If the heart rate has slowed down significantly -- and babies have a much faster heart rate normally than older people -- we would give adrenaline in that situation, particularly if you could not feel a pulse.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Dealing with the NNU, was the use of adrenaline in these circumstances a commonplace occurrence?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, it's not common to give adrenaline. It was becoming more common as events continued on the unit with repeated collapses of babies.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: But generally?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Generally not, no. Until 2015, uncommon.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: At what stage did you arrive by way of [Baby H]'s resuscitation, do you recall?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, I recall by having read the notes. I think, if we look at the note, I think I wrote down that I was called at about 3.30 in the morning and arrived at 3.36.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Let's go to the note rather than ask you to guess. 262, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: But a lot of my recall of what happened 7 years ago is based on what I wrote or others wrote about me or events at the time --
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Of course.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- than having a vivid memory of exactly what was going on 7 years ago.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Perhaps if we could go down a little bit nearer the top.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We can see there on the left is a list of times. This represents -- I think we've seen it before -- a resuscitation in the way in which they're recorded in the medical notes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. If you wouldn't mind, just the top there, where Dr Ventress, the registrar, has written that on my arrival, being bagged and so on. That means Dr Ventress wasn't on the neonatal unit at the time and that's why I wouldn't have been there because she wouldn't have had to start intervening if I was there. I wouldn't have been there standing there doing nothing, so I think she was called urgently to the unit and then that's why I think I had gone home after inserting the chest drain and then I was called back in.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right, okay. If we go down to the entry at 3.35, that's certainly when Dr Ventress records your arrival. If we go down to your note, please, next, which is more important, could you take us through your note, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Right. I was called in from home at around 3.30.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Arrived 3.36. Dr Ventress had just put down it was 3.35. I don't think that minute makes much difference.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: CPR, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, was in progress.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That means [Baby H] was being ventilated, not with the ventilator anymore, but through the Neopuff, through the
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: endotracheal tube, and I think the jury know all about the Neopuff now.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes. So disconnected from the ventilation and physically being done by a nurse using -- I think we've seen a device with a button on the top; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, but the breathing was being done for [Baby H] through her endotracheal tube that was still in her windpipe.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: And also, someone would have been pressing -- I can't remember who -- pressing regularly on her chest to help circulation. Then I say that [Baby H] appeared pale, there was no pulse to be felt when the chest was compressed.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Sorry, no pulse when chest compression stopped. And then I put in brackets "femoral". This meant feeling the femoral pulse, which is the pulse at the top of the leg, a large artery that you can feel a pulse through.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: When someone stopped pressing on [Baby H]'s chest, you couldn't feel a pulse. And obviously, the whole point of pressing on the chest is to try to stimulate and provide some circulation. So when someone was pressing on her chest, there was a pulse. When someone stopped pressing on her chest briefly, there was no pulse. This is why we say she was in cardiac arrest.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. You then go on to describe a bradycardia?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So bradycardia means a slow heart rate on the monitor, 50 to 70, and for babies it should be well above 100. Sinus bradycardia is just a type of bradycardia, an abnormally slow heart rate. Then I say:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Had been given adrenaline, two doses".
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I think two doses on my arrival. It would have been around the time I arrived, she'd already been given two doses.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then the cold light was used. Because we knew that [Baby H] had suffered a whole series of tension pneumothoraces, so we performed the cold light again.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: No evidence of a pneumothorax. Having already explained a very small pneumothorax may not be detected with a cold light, a life-threatening pneumothorax is a tension pneumothorax and it ought to show on a cold light. So the cold light did not suggest there was a tension pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I undertook a limited cardio echo. I am not -- I was not at that stage particularly expert at doing cardiac echoes, but this was just to check whether there was an abnormal amount of fluid collected around the heart, no more detailed assessment of the heart. I say here there was no obvious pericardial fluid, meaning fluid around the heart, because that can cause cardiac arrest and that could be the result of trauma, for example chest drains that had been pushed against the heart, but the ultrasound did not show that that had happened.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I say in brackets:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Tiny rim of [query] air against the left side of heart."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the ultrasound, the cardiac echo, did suggest a black line against the heart, and that could be air, but it would only be a tiny amount of air and we already know the cold light did not show that there was any significant tension pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: This is an emergency situation. [Baby H]'s in cardiac arrest. I said the best way of detecting a pneumothorax, tension or otherwise, is the chest X-ray. There is no time to do a chest X-ray when you're trying to save a little baby's life, so we had to rely on cold light. Ultrasound can be done very quickly, we have the machine on the unit and we get the image immediately.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. So the cardiac echo. What sort of device is that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: An ultrasound machine.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That is the ultrasound machine?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. It is a cardiac ultrasound. An image of the heart using ultrasound.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you. Further bolus of adrenaline?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. This is the third one now that was given, so two just before I arrived, a third one after my arrival, and then a medication called atropine, which isn't often used in cardiac arrest situations, it's sometimes used and it helps to speed up the heart. The reason that was given is we had already given [Baby H] two doses of adrenaline, this was the third one. Adrenaline speeds up the heart but, very importantly, also makes a contraction stronger. Atropine just helps to speed up the heart rate and I felt that may help [Baby H].
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Okay. You've given a measurement there rounded up.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Is that to 60?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, 60 micrograms. It's 20 micrograms per kilogram, but [Baby H] was only about 2.5 kg, but rounded it up to 60 micrograms. The exact dose isn't vital. Giving the right drug is very important. Then at this stage we now have a spontaneous output. By "spontaneous" I mean it didn't require someone pressing on [Baby H]'s heart. When you stopped pressing on her chest -- when you stopped pressing on her chest now you could feel pulses, so she was producing her own pulses.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Her heart was working again?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. The heart rate increased to 160 after 22 minutes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That's not from giving these medications now, it's from the bradycardia first starting, but I wasn't there when it first started, I'm going by Dr Ventress' recollection of when it first started.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That 22 minutes is from the start of the resuscitation process?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, the start of the cardiac arrest and resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Until the point where you've detected spontaneous --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Spontaneous heart rate at a good rate of 160.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: That gives us an idea of how long this went on.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. But 22 minutes without a cardiac output would be catastrophic, really, and likely to cause severe brain damage if no one was doing anything. Fortunately, [Baby H] had been given cardiopulmonary resuscitation. She was being ventilated, she was given a circulation by someone pressing on her heart, and that's why hopefully she hadn't been compromised by having a cardiac arrest or very slow heart rate for 22 minutes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. You then go on to make some post-CPR recordings; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. The heart rate is remaining good, high-ish, 170 to 190. It wouldn't be unexpected for the heart rate to be even slightly faster than usual after the doses of adrenaline and atropine, and, importantly, [Baby H] was making good respiratory effort, which is very good because she was being ventilated
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: before she collapsed with a cardiac arrest, but she's actually making her own respiratory efforts now:
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: "Fair AE [air entry] bilaterally."
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I've put "crackles on the left". So there was reasonable air entry both sides of her chest. If she had a tension pneumothorax you wouldn't hear -- you'd expect to hear little or no air entry on that side of the chest. So it's reassuring there is air entry on both sides of the chest, but a bit crackly, meaning probably secretions in the lung on the left side.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: So the cold light has suggested no pneumothorax at this point or no significant -- is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I -- sorry, yes. Well, slightly earlier -- have I got control? Going back up my -- I said there was cold light, no evidence of a pneumothorax. And then it's probably some minutes later, recording these observations here, the postcardiopulmonary resuscitation. So a few minutes earlier, no pneumothorax on cold light. I don't think we did another cold light -- I haven't recorded doing another cold light examination here. I'm just saying by listening to the chest and the fact she's only requiring 30% oxygen, remembering before the third chest drain she needed 70 to 80% oxygen, now only 30% means it's very unlikely there's a tension pneumothorax there.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. Your next entry, is it "colour"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Colour is now pink and only requiring 30% oxygen".
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Now I'm trying to work out why [Baby H]'s arrested. We know she's had three tension pneumothoraces, requiring three chest drains at night, and it's unclear, but this is a cardio -this is a cardiac arrest without any obvious pneumothorax and certainly without a tension pneumothorax. So why had [Baby H] suffered this cardiac arrest? I'm saying it's unclear why she had, but it began with a desaturation, so oxygen levels dropping.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right. That's what I wanted to confirm, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: But can I just point out on this X-ray, you cannot tell from this view how close it is to the heart.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: No. It could be very close or it might not be.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Right, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I just have one matter. I really, I think, need Mr Myers' assistance in relation to this first of all. It's just this, Mr Myers: are you putting to the doctor that by reason of the various medical problems that [Baby H] had experienced and the procedures that had been carried out that the emergency that required the resuscitation at about 3.30 that morning was a consequence of what had gone before and the medical procedures and was not attributable to her having another pneumothorax, tension pneumothorax?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: As for the procedure, which Dr Gibbs has engaged in, that was to deal with the situation as he saw as he has described it to us.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I just want to be clear so I know what it is that's being put. I think that maybe where Dr Gibbs was having difficulty in the question. So I just wanted to see if we could clarify it and then, if necessary, Dr Gibbs can answer that point if that is the point. It may be that I'm misunderstanding the point.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I am just looking at the accumulation of treatment that [Baby H] had received, looking at the position of the drains in the course of the time they were there, and therefore looking at what took place at each stage. I wasn't questioning whether or not there was a pneumothorax that needed to be drained. We're not debating that. Plainly, in the views of Dr Gibbs, there was a reason to insert the drain and we don't suggest he was wrong to do so.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: No, no. I knew you weren't suggesting that.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We don't give the same clean bill of health to everything that happened to [Baby H] during this. We've looked at what Dr Jayaram did and we're interested in that in that context. So we're interested in looking at what happens with that second drain, where it goes and what it could have done, and we're also interested in looking -- and we say it's important to consider the whole picture with [Baby H]. Of course, we heard the clinicians say many times, don't just take one or two things, look at the whole picture. That's what we're doing over those 3 days, my Lord. So we're looking at the cumulative effect, or what could be the cumulative effect, of all the procedures she underwent upon her.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So that could be responsible for the actual emergency situation. I needn't go through what it was because we've had it rehearsed in evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's what --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: So --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: And my response to that, my Lord, is that it is true, Mr Myers is correct, it is true that repeated procedures and having three chest drains inserted into the chest, and repeated intubations because of a blocked tube, adds a stress to a neonate. But each one was done for a very good, important reason. At the end of all of that was after I'd put the third chest drain in, before I went home, before being called back an hour or two later.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: She was stable, her oxygen had come down and then she deteriorated an hour or two later. So I don't think you can say that having repeated chest drains was the reason she deteriorated at 3 in the morning because after all those chest drains, and I put the last one in, she was stable, oxygenation had come down, and why then would she suddenly deteriorate a couple of hours later?
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I don't think it's tenable to say it's the stress of all the previous episodes. She was in a good condition at the end of the third of those chest drains.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I make it plain, my Lord. We certainly don't accept for one minute that the mere fact an hour went by before it happened explains that at all. These things can happen unexpectedly and in far less dramatic circumstances than what was going on with [Baby H].
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That's where we are with this.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: But in that hour that went by --
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: Well, I don't think we --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: There was another pneumothorax. Dr Ventress had confirmed that.
blocks.speaker: GIBBS

blocks.text: I think we understand where the differences lie now and what Mr Myers is suggesting and what your response is.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, my Lord. Anything further?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. Thank you very much, Dr Gibbs.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: You will be returning later in the trial, so please remember what I said to you before. Don't talk to anyone about this case or anything to do with this case, any of the patients concerned. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The witness withdrew)
My Lord, I'm afraid that's as far as we can go this afternoon.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Oh, we're not having anything read?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, there's been a change.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Well, I did say yesterday there was a prospect we might finish slightly earlier today and I've been proved right. So that's it for today and obviously for this week. 10.30 on Monday morning, please, when we will continue.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Just so that the jury know, I think it's anticipated that we will complete the evidence in relation to [Baby H] on Tuesday.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Tuesday afternoon, we think.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. That's so you know how we're proceeding. Then we'll move on to the next baby after that. Thank you very much. Please, of course, remember your obligations. No research, no conversations with anyone unless you're all together. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)
Mr Myers, will someone want to see --
Yes, we're grateful, my Lord, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Someone will be down very shortly.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS
